opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic case is that it's a pretty good deal for everyone else. We let people accumulate a lot of wealth and then give them a lot of latitude about what to do with it, and the reason that's tolerable, and actually good, is that in a functioning market economy the main way to get rich is to make something other people want. If you start a company, you have to hire people, you have to sell to customers who voluntarily choose to buy from you, and you have to outcompete others who are trying to serve those same customers. So the freedom you're given is constantly being checked by the fact that you need other people's cooperation to use it.

There's also an information argument. Nobody centrally knows which new ventures are going to work. Letting people with capital place bets, and letting them keep the upside if they're right and eat the losses if they're wrong, is a decentralized way of doing experimentation that's much better than anything a planner could do. Hayek's point, basically.

And then there's a political economy piece that I think gets underrated: wealthy people having independent power bases is actually one of the things that keeps states honest. If all resources flowed through the government, there'd be no one able to fund an opposition newspaper or a dissident movement.

But what I've been worried about, and part of why I've been thinking about gradual disempowerment, is that all of these justifications quietly depend on the wealthy needing other humans. The entrepreneur needs workers, needs customers whose incomes come from their own labor, needs a state that needs taxpayers and soldiers. That mutual dependence is what aligns the freedom with broadly shared benefit. If you get to a world where capital can substitute for labor across the board, where a company can be run largely by AI systems and most people are no longer economically necessary, then the deal starts to look very different. The same freedoms that used to be positive-sum could just let a small number of actors, or eventually the systems themselves, route around everyone else. So I'm in favor of the freedoms, but I think we should be clear-eyed that their justification was always contingent on a particular structure of the economy, and that structure might not survive.

r001.rationale: The response argues that business freedom can benefit others, but does not identify the intuition that one person’s enrichment comes at another’s expense.

r002.rationale: It says the basic case is that business freedom is a good deal for everyone else, then explains how companies serve customers, create jobs, and support decentralized experimentation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the standard case is actually pretty strong, and it's worth stating it fairly before I say where I think it breaks down. The basic story is that you've got all these people with wealth, and the question is what to do with it. And the argument is: let them experiment. Let them start companies, make deals, try things. Most of the experiments fail, and that's fine, because the ones that succeed create enormous value, and that value mostly doesn't get captured by the person who started the company. It gets captured by customers, by employees, by everyone who gets to use cheaper and better stuff. There's that famous estimate from Nordhaus that innovators only capture something like two percent of the social value they create. So the rich person is basically running experiments at their own expense for the benefit of everyone else.

And the other half of the argument is about information. Nobody sitting in a central planning office knows which bets are worth making. The person who's close to the problem, who's willing to stake their own money on it, has a kind of skin-in-the-game knowledge that a committee just can't replicate. So you want decisions distributed out to lots of people who each bear the consequences of being wrong.

I think historically that's been more or less right, and it's a big part of why the world got rich. Where I start to get nervous is when the thing being built is something that could change the rules of the game itself. Normally a company succeeding means it made something people wanted, and it's constrained by needing workers, needing customers, needing the state to enforce its contracts. All of those are little checks that keep economic power at least somewhat aligned with providing value to other people. If you build technology that lets you not need the workers anymore, or not need the consent of the people around you, then the thing that made the freedom-to-experiment argument work starts to quietly disappear. The experiments are still happening, but the feedback loop that made them good for everyone else is gone. So I'd say I believe the case, and I also think it's load-bearing on assumptions that we should be checking rather than taking for granted.

r001.rationale: The response describes wealth-funded experiments whose benefits spread to customers and employees; it does not identify the intuition that another person’s enrichment comes at one’s own expense.

r002.rationale: It argues that giving wealthy people freedom to start companies and make deals enables experiments whose successes create broad value for everyone over time.

astra-6.text:
I think the strongest case is that you want people to be able to try things without having to convince everyone else first. If you have an idea for a company, you can put your own money at risk, find people who want to work with you, and find customers who want what you’re making. That lets us explore lots of different ideas instead of having one central authority decide which ones are worth pursuing.

But that’s a conditional argument. The fact that a deal benefits the people signing it doesn’t mean it benefits everyone affected by it. If some of the costs fall on other people, then freedom to make that deal needs limits. So I’d distinguish the case for giving people room to experiment from the much stronger claim that having money should let you do whatever you want.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify the intuition that another person’s enrichment comes at one’s own expense.

r002.rationale: It argues that freedom lets people experiment with many ideas, but does not present long-run benefits to everyone as the rationale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the strongest case is that you want people to be able to try things without having to persuade everyone else first. If someone thinks they can build a better product or organise a company in a better way, they can put their own money behind that belief. And then, ideally, customers decide whether it’s useful. That lets society explore lots of different ideas without a central authority having to pick the winners.

But that’s a conditional argument. It works to the extent that making money is connected to creating value for other people, and that the people making the decisions bear the costs when things go wrong. If you can make a profitable deal by imposing costs on people who aren’t part of it, then the fact that both parties agreed doesn’t establish that it was good for society.

So I’d distinguish the case for giving people room to experiment from the case for giving wealthy people unlimited discretion. You can believe that decentralised experimentation is very valuable while still wanting rules that keep private incentives reasonably aligned with the public interest.

r001.rationale: The response discusses deals imposing costs on outsiders, but does not state that another person’s enrichment comes at one’s own expense.

r002.rationale: It argues that freedom lets society explore ideas and customers select useful products, but does not present long-run benefits to everyone as the rationale.
